findings.evidence: The diff removes `msys2/setup-msys2@v2`, which installed `mingw-w64-${{matrix.msysenv}}-gcc` for each arch. Now the build relies only on `mingw_prefix=C:/mingw32` (line 144) and `C:/mingw64` (line 132). No step installs these toolchains or verifies they exist, and windows.py:82 just builds `prefix = env["mingw_prefix"] + "/bin/"` and calls `i686-w64-mingw32-g++`. If the runner image has no 32-bit MinGW at C:/mingw32, the release artefact godot-angle-static-x86_32-gcc-release is never produced.

members.claim: As far as I know, the windows-2025 runner image comes with a 64-bit MinGW in C:\mingw64 but no 32-bit i686 toolchain in C:\mingw32. MSYS2 used to install mingw-w64-i686-gcc for this job, and nothing replaces that step now. With mingw_prefix=C:/mingw32, SCons will call C:/mingw32/bin/i686-w64-mingw32-g++, which most likely doesn't exist, so the x86_32 GCC build and its release artifact will fail. Add an explicit step that installs an i686 MinGW toolchain, for example a pinned niXman/winlibs i686 msvcrt archive.

members.claim: The GCC toolchain is now whatever MinGW the runner image happens to ship, and its version and CRT can change whenever GitHub updates the image. These artifacts are labelled 'MSVCRT'. The workflow doesn't pin or check that the preinstalled toolchain targets msvcrt rather than ucrt, or that it ships the prefixed x86_64-w64-mingw32-* binaries (including gcc-ar) that windows.py requires. If any of that changes, the build could break, or the shipped libraries could quietly become incompatible with what users link them against. Download a pinned toolchain instead, as the llvm-mingw step already does.
